title: Has the Online Safety Act been implemented to keep children safe?
label: 3 November 2026 · Online Safety Act implementation
summary: Former lawmakers, an internet law academic and a children’s rights campaigner told the committee the Online Safety Act still has the right overall approach but has been limited by how Ofcom has interpreted and applied it. They agreed the Act could do more on platform design, proactive scanning and enforcement, and proposed a mix of clearer interpretation, better use of existing powers, stronger enforcement tools, civil routes to redress and improved parliamentary scrutiny.

speakers.label: Damian Collins
speakers.name: Damian Collins
speakers.role: Former MP and Chair, Joint Committee on the Draft Online Safety Bill

speakers.label: Professor Lorna Woods
speakers.name: Professor Lorna Woods OBE
speakers.role: Emeritus Professor of Internet Law, University of Essex

speakers.label: Sir Jeremy Wright
speakers.name: Sir Jeremy Wright KC MP
speakers.role: Member for Kenilworth and Southam; former Secretary of State for DCMS

glossary.definition: The UK communications regulator responsible for enforcing the Online Safety Act.
A legal protection that shields platforms from further regulatory action if they follow the regulator’s codes.
A standard that would require platforms to take reasonable, proportionate steps to keep users safe.
Ofcom’s detailed rules that explain how services should meet the Act’s duties.
How a platform identifies and evaluates the risks its design or content pose to users.
Sanctions that affect a company’s wider operations, not just fines—such as cutting off ancillary services.
Government powers to change primary legislation by secondary measures without a new Act of Parliament.
Digital Services Act, the EU law that also regulates big online platforms.
A specialist examination Ofcom can commission to investigate a company’s systems and practices.
Existing criminal offences listed in the Act that form the basis for enforcing illegal harms.

chapters.title: Opening assessment: Act’s potential and present results
chapters.takeaway: All witnesses say the Act’s approach can work, but Ofcom’s interpretation and lack of enforcement mean early evidence shows little change in children’s exposure to harm.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Ofcom’s recent report shows little change in children’s exposure to harmful content nine months after the children’s duties began. Does the Act still have the potential to meet its aims, or does it need fundamental reform?

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: I think the Act still has potential. We chose a principles-based duty-of-care approach rather than fixed rules because rules get out of date fast. The problem is implementation: Ofcom could use the law more assertively than it has.

turns.speaker: Professor Lorna Woods
turns.text: I agree. Duty of care and design-based obligations were the right idea because companies control platform design. My worry is how far Ofcom was prepared to go without a clearer legislative steer.

turns.speaker: Damian Collins
turns.text: The Act hasn’t delivered because Ofcom’s interpretation of its powers—especially whether platforms must proactively scan for illegal content—has been too narrow. Parliament intended platforms to identify and reduce illegal content, not wait for complaints.

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: I broadly agree. The Ofcom report is unacceptable to desperate parents. The issues are: how Ofcom interprets its powers, gaps the government didn’t foresee, Ofcom’s culture and urgency, and insufficient enforcement powers.

chapters.title: Safe harbour and codes of practice
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses disagree about safe harbour: some see a useful protection if it drives ambition; others say it has been interpreted as a low bar that blocks progress.

turns.speaker: The Lord Bishop of Winchester
turns.text: Some say safe harbour has become a ceiling rather than a floor for platforms. Is that right and should it be changed?

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: Yes. Safe harbour has been read as: do everything in the code and you’re fine. That leaves risks outside the codes unaddressed and locks in low standards.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: I partly disagree. Safe harbour can be fair in a fast-moving sector, but Ofcom’s expectations are too low. Safe harbour should reward ambitious, proportionate safety work, not freeze companies at the status quo.

turns.speaker: Damian Collins
turns.text: We designed the Act so codes would give certainty, but not cap obligations. The intention was that codes are a floor; Ofcom’s interpretation shouldn’t let platforms hide behind a minimum standard.

turns.speaker: Professor Lorna Woods
turns.text: The issue is how detailed the codes are. Ofcom seems to have focused on steps it can precisely measure—a tick-box approach—instead of programmatic obligations requiring companies to try their best to reduce harm.

chapters.title: Duty of care, safety-by-design and addiction
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses want stronger emphasis on platform design (recommender systems, dark patterns, extended use) and many argue the Act already allows this if Ofcom applies it ambitiously.

turns.speaker: Lord Holmes of Richmond
turns.text: Was an overarching duty of care feasible? Parliamentary counsel reportedly had doubts—was that right?

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: I think it was viable and should have been tried. An overarching duty of care—like health and safety law—would set a clear expectation that platforms do what they reasonably can to keep users safe.

turns.speaker: Professor Lorna Woods
turns.text: I can’t see a technical reason it wouldn’t work; other sectors use broad duties. The problem is that focus on content overtook design and lifecycle issues during the Bill’s passage.

turns.speaker: Damian Collins
turns.text: We worried what a duty of care would rest on—Human Rights Act, EU Charter, existing offences. The compromise was to base duties on listed priority legal offences so Parliament decides what’s illegal and Ofcom enforces it.

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: Parliament didn’t fully grasp how the technology works; the Act’s language on 'content and activity' got narrowed to content. Safety-by-design should be central; there’s an engineering standard (IEEE 2089) that helps define it.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: If we adopt a safety-by-design code, what concrete changes would platforms have to make, and can Ofcom do that now or would legislation be needed?

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Many things are already in the Act—'functionality' and risk assessments include features that keep children online longer. Ofcom could require platforms to address those risks now if it chose to.

turns.speaker: Damian Collins
turns.text: The Act already regulates feeds and intermediary liability; it should be clear there’s no safe way to recommend self-harm content to a teen. Platforms can and do alter feeds; the law should require them to design feeds to avoid illegal or clearly harmful outcomes.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: Ofcom says 'addiction' isn’t a defined harm. Should addiction or 'extended use' be added into the Act so Ofcom must address it?

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Section 11(6)(f) already asks platforms to consider features that affect how much children use a service—for example autoplay. That covers extended use even if 'addiction' isn’t named; better use of that clause would help.

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: I’d make 'extended use' explicit rather than defining 'addiction'. Ofcom should treat dark patterns and features that keep kids online as risks to be mitigated under safe-by-design.

chapters.title: Enforcement, sanctions and civil routes
chapters.takeaway: All witnesses want Ofcom to use stronger enforcement and evidence tools; many recommend civil claims or product-liability-style remedies alongside regulatory powers.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: Can Ofcom use business disruption measures effectively, and are fines enough?

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Yes, business disruption measures should be used when justified. The maximum fine (10% of global turnover) is serious. But these measures have hardly been used, so we don’t yet know their practical deterrent effect.

turns.speaker: Professor Lorna Woods
turns.text: Courts will want a strong evidence threshold before allowing business disruption. Ancillary-service measures may be more useful than cutting access, but evidence thresholds for interim steps may need adjustment.

turns.speaker: Damian Collins
turns.text: Fines aren’t the only lever. We recommended clearer civil routes to allow victims or groups to sue—class actions or consumer redress—because US courts have shown courts can force systemic change and disclosure companies resist in regulatory processes.

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: Families have nowhere to go now. Ofcom sometimes treats urgent problems as 'horizon-scanning' rather than urgent enforcement. We should expand enforcement tools, consider an e-safety commissioner for individuals, and explore digital product liability.

turns.speaker: Damian Collins
turns.text: Also note the 'skilled person’s report' power in the Act—a forensic investigation tool similar to court discovery. Ofcom could use it more to expose company practices, but it hasn’t been widely used.

chapters.title: Priorities and parliamentary scrutiny
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses’ top priorities are clearer interpretation and use of the Act, stronger enforcement (including civil redress), safety-by-design, and better parliamentary oversight such as a permanent joint committee.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: One priority each: what should the committee recommend to improve the UK’s online safety regime? Say if it needs secondary legislation, new laws, or can be done under the current framework.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Use what we’ve got first. Ofcom should be pushed to be bolder within the Act before seeking new primary legislation. At the same time, set up stronger parliamentary scrutiny—like a permanent Joint Committee—to follow fast-moving regulation.

turns.speaker: Professor Lorna Woods
turns.text: I have a list of ten practical fixes I’ll send the committee. In short: clarify rules and evidence expectations, stop backsliding on protections, and tidy up the existing framework rather than rewrite it immediately.

turns.speaker: Damian Collins
turns.text: Fix Ofcom’s narrower interpretation of proactive duties and increase use of skilled-person investigations. Create clearer routes for civil redress and class actions so victims can seek compensation and force disclosure.

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: My one priority: Ofcom must enforce every risk in its risk register—mitigate, manage or forbid it. Use government direction, existing powers, Henry VIII powers if needed, and strengthen routes to help individuals.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Please send your lists, quotes and detailed proposals to the committee. We will continue scrutiny, then hear from Ofcom and ministers before issuing recommendations early next year.
